name: ATTINY13A-SSUR
title: ATtiny13A: 8-bit AVR microcontroller, 1 KB flash, 64 B EEPROM, 64 B SRAM, 10-bit ADC, 1.8-5.5 V, 20 MHz
summary: ATtiny13A is an 8-bit AVR RISC microcontroller with 1 KB of in-system self-programmable flash, 64 bytes of EEPROM and 64 bytes of SRAM, six I/O lines on Port B, one 8-bit Timer/Counter with two PWM outputs, a four-input 10-bit ADC with a 1.1 V internal reference, an analog comparator and a watchdog clocked by its own 128 kHz oscillator. It runs from 1.8 V to 5.5 V, at up to 4 MHz from 1.8 V, 10 MHz from 2.7 V and 20 MHz from 4.5 V, clocked by its calibrated 9.6/4.8 MHz RC oscillator, the 128 kHz oscillator or an external clock. It is programmed over SPI or by 12 V high-voltage serial programming and debugged through debugWIRE on the RESET pin. Packages are 8-pin PDIP and SOIC (ATtiny13A-SSUR is the 150-mil JEDEC SOIC on tape and reel) and 10- and 20-pad MLF.
key_figures: AVR 8-bit RISC, up to 20 MIPS at 20 MHz
1 KB flash, 64 B EEPROM, 64 B SRAM

notes: Suffix letters: H or 7 NiPdAu lead finish; U, N or F matte tin; R tape and reel.
Every package is Pb-free, halide-free, fully green and RoHS compliant.
Topside marking of the 10M1 parts: line 1 T13, line 2 Axx, line 3 xxx.
Packages: 8P3 8-lead 0.300" wide PDIP; 8S2 8-lead 0.209" wide EIAJ SOIC; 8S1 8-lead 0.150" wide JEDEC SOIC; 20M1 20-pad 4 x 4 x 0.8 mm MLF, 0.50 mm pitch; 10M1 10-pad 3 x 3 x 1 mm MLF, 0.50 mm pitch.

circuits.title: External clock drive configuration
circuits.description: An external clock source drives CLKI (PB3); its return is the part's ground. CKSEL[1:0] must be 00 for this clock to be used.

circuits.title: debugWIRE setup
circuits.description: The debugger's single dW wire joins the RESET pin (PB5); the part runs from 1.8 V to 5.5 V. A 10 kΩ to 20 kΩ pull-up on the dW line is optional; RESET must not be tied straight to VCC, reset capacitors must be removed and any other reset source disconnected while debugging.

circuits.title: Serial programming and verify
circuits.description: In-system programming over SPI: the programmer holds RESET (PB5) low and clocks SCK into PB2, sends data into MOSI (PB0) and reads MISO (PB1). Supply 1.8 V to 5.5 V. Running from the internal oscillator, CLKI needs no clock source.

circuits.title: High-voltage serial programming
circuits.description: High-voltage serial programming: 11.5 V to 12.5 V on PB5 (RESET), the part supplied with 1.8 V to 5.5 V, clock into SCI (PB3), instructions into SII (PB1), data into SDI (PB0) and data out of SDO (PB2).

operation.text: An 8-bit AVR RISC microcontroller with 1 KB of self-programmable flash, 64 bytes each of EEPROM and SRAM, six I/O lines, an 8-bit timer with two PWM outputs, a 4-channel 10-bit ADC, an analog comparator and a watchdog with its own oscillator. It runs at up to 4 MHz from 1.8 V, 10 MHz from 2.7 V and 20 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V. Most instructions take one clock, so throughput is close to 1 MIPS per MHz.

Harvard machine with a one-stage pipeline: the next instruction is fetched while the current one executes. The 32 working registers all feed the ALU, so a two-register operation finishes in one clock. R26-R31 pair up as the 16-bit X, Y and Z pointers; Z also addresses tables in flash. Instructions are 16 or 32 bits. The status register is not saved automatically on an interrupt.

The stack lives in SRAM and grows downward; SPL is the only stack pointer register. At power-on reset it points to the last SRAM address, and it must be kept above 0x60. PUSH and POP move it by one, calls, returns and interrupts by two.

An interrupt takes at least four clocks to reach its vector, during which the program counter is pushed; the usual jump at the vector takes three more. A multi-cycle instruction in progress finishes first. Waking from sleep adds four clocks on top of the start-up time. RETI takes four clocks and sets the I bit again. After RETI, and after SEI, one more instruction runs before a pending interrupt is served. Lower vector addresses have higher priority; RESET is highest, then INT0.

Flash is 512 x 16 bits, addressed by a 9-bit program counter (0x0000-0x01FF). Data space: 0x0000-0x001F registers, 0x0020-0x005F the 64 I/O registers, 0x0060-0x009F the 64 bytes of SRAM. SRAM is reached in two clocks. Indirect addressing with displacement reaches 63 locations beyond the Y or Z base.

IN and OUT use I/O addresses 0x00-0x3F; as data space with LD and ST the same registers sit 0x20 higher. Registers 0x00-0x1F are bit-addressable by SBI, CBI, SBIS and SBIC. Some flags clear when a one is written to them; on this part SBI and CBI touch only the named bit, so they are safe on such registers.

The 64-byte EEPROM is byte-addressed (EEARL, 0-63) and rated for 100,000 write/erase cycles. A write needs EEMPE set and then EEPE set within four clocks; EEPM[1:0] picks atomic erase-and-write (3.4 ms), erase only or write only (1.8 ms each). A read stalls the CPU four clocks, a write two. EEPE stays set until the write ends, and no other EEPROM access works meanwhile. Write timing comes from the calibrated RC oscillator. An EEPROM write also blocks SPM and firmware reads of the fuses and lock bits.

A too-low supply can corrupt EEPROM or flash, either because the write itself fails or because the CPU misexecutes. Holding the part in reset through low supply, with the brown-out detector or an external supervisor, prevents it; a write already running completes if the supply allows. For flash, sleeping in power-down through low supply also protects it.

The selected source feeds separate CPU, I/O, flash and ADC clock domains that sleep modes stop selectively. Sources (CKSEL fuses): external clock on CLKI, the calibrated RC oscillator at 9.6 or 4.8 MHz, or the 128 kHz oscillator. The reset delay is timed by the watchdog oscillator; SUT fuses set it to 14 CK, 14 CK + 4 ms or 14 CK + 64 ms.
Parts ship with CKSEL = 10, SUT = 10 and CKDIV8 programmed: the 9.6 MHz RC oscillator divided by 8, with the longest start-up delay.

Selected with CKSEL = 00. The period may vary by at most 2% between consecutive cycles; larger steps can make the part misbehave, so hold it in reset while changing frequency, or use the system clock prescaler instead.

The RC oscillator is nominal at 3 V and 25 °C and needs no external parts. At reset the 9.6 MHz calibration byte is loaded into OSCCAL; 4.8 MHz mode differs only by an internal divider, and its own calibration byte has to be copied in by firmware. OSCCAL 0x00 gives the lowest and 0x7F the highest frequency. Change OSCCAL by no more than 0x20 at a time. When EEPROM or flash is written, keep the frequency no more than 10% above nominal, or the write can fail. Calibration is intended for 9.6 or 4.8 MHz only.
A low-power oscillator whose frequency varies with supply, temperature and batch. It can be the system clock (CKSEL = 11) and always clocks the watchdog and reset delay.

CLKPR divides the system clock by 1 to 256 at run time. To change it, write CLKPCE = 1 with the other bits 0, then write CLKPS within four clocks with CLKPCE = 0; interrupts should be off meanwhile. CKDIV8 sets the reset value to divide-by-8 (0011) or 1 (0000). Switching produces no glitch and no intermediate frequency above the old or new one.

SE in MCUCR set and a SLEEP instruction enter the mode chosen by SM[1:0]. Idle stops the CPU and flash clocks only. ADC Noise Reduction also stops the I/O clock, leaving the ADC, external interrupts and watchdog running. Power-down stops the oscillator; only external reset, watchdog, brown-out, an INT0 level interrupt or a pin change wakes it. On wake the part waits the start-up time plus four clocks, runs the interrupt, and continues after SLEEP with registers and SRAM intact. A level interrupt used to wake from power-down must last until start-up ends.

With BOD enabled by fuse, it can be switched off for the duration of power-down sleep: write BODS and BODSE to one, then within four clocks BODS = 1 and BODSE = 0, and execute SLEEP within three clocks while BODS is active. BOD comes back on at wake-up, which then takes about 60 µs.

PRR stops the clock to Timer/Counter0 (PRTIM0) or the ADC (PRADC), freezing the module and its registers; clearing the bit resumes it where it stopped. Disable the ADC before shutting it down; the analog comparator is unusable while the ADC is shut down.

Turn off the ADC before sleeping (the next conversion is then an extended one), the analog comparator (and its bandgap input), the BOD and the watchdog when not needed: each runs in every sleep mode. The internal reference stays on while BOD, the comparator bandgap input or the ADC needs it. Input buffers are shut off in sleep modes that stop both the I/O and ADC clocks, except on pins used for wake-up. A floating input or one near VCC/2 draws excess current; disable digital inputs on analog pins with DIDR0.

Power-on reset (below VPOT), external reset (RESET low longer than tRST, works without a clock), watchdog reset (a one-clock pulse at time-out) and brown-out reset (VCC below VBOT for longer than tBOD while BOD is enabled). Ports go to their reset state at once; after the last source releases, the delay counter holds reset for the SUT/CKSEL time-out. MCUSR records which source acted; PORF clears only by writing zero.

The 1.1 V bandgap serves the BOD and can be the comparator input or the ADC reference. It is powered only while BOD is enabled, ACBG is set or the ADC is on; after turning it on, allow its start-up time before using the result.

Counts the 128 kHz oscillator; time-outs from 16 ms to 8 s. Modes: interrupt (useful to wake from sleep), system reset, or interrupt first then reset. WDTON programmed forces reset mode. Clearing WDE or changing the prescaler needs WDCE and WDE written to one together, then the new value within four clocks. WDRF forces WDE on, so clear WDRF and WDE early in start-up code even when the watchdog is not used. Reset the watchdog before shortening its period.

INT0 triggers on low level, any change, falling or rising edge (ISC0[1:0]); any of PCINT[5:0] enabled in PCMSK raises the pin change interrupt. Both fire even when the pin is an output. Pin change and INT0 low level are detected without a clock and wake the part from any sleep mode; INT0 edges need the I/O clock. An edge or change must last longer than one clock period to be caught.

Each pin has DDxn (direction), PORTxn (output value or pull-up enable) and PINxn (input); writing one to PINxn toggles PORTxn. PUD in MCUCR disables every pull-up. Pins are tri-stated at reset even with no clock. Every pin has protection diodes to VCC and ground and can drive LEDs directly. Input reads pass a synchronizer, adding ½ to 1½ clocks of delay; reading back a value just written needs a NOP between OUT and IN. Going between tri-state and output high passes through pull-up or output low.

Give unused pins a defined level, most simply with the internal pull-up (off during reset). Where reset current matters, fit an external pull resistor (up or down). Tying a pin directly to VCC or GND risks a large current if it is ever set as an output.

Programming RSTDISBL turns PB5 into a weak I/O; from then on only high-voltage serial programming can change the fuses. With RSTDISBL programmed the reset delay for the internal oscillators grows to 14 CK + 4 ms.

An 8-bit counter with two double-buffered compare units (OC0A on PB0, OC0B on PB1) and interrupts on overflow and each compare match. Modes: normal (TOP 0xFF), CTC (TOP = OCR0A), fast PWM and phase correct PWM, each with TOP 0xFF or OCR0A. The clock comes from clkI/O through the prescaler (1, 8, 64, 256, 1024) or from the T0 pin. A CPU write to TCNT0 blocks a compare match on the next timer clock. FOC0x forces a compare in non-PWM modes without setting the flag. OC0x reaches the pin only with its DDR bit set. In CTC mode OCR0A is not buffered, so a new value below TCNT0 misses a match and the counter wraps through 0xFF.

Fast PWM: OCR0A at BOTTOM gives a narrow spike each MAX+1 timer clocks, OCR0A at MAX a constant level; COM0A = 1 with WGM02 set toggles OC0A for a 50% square wave of up to fclk_I/O/2. Phase correct PWM: OCR0A at BOTTOM holds the non-inverted output low, at MAX high. Phase correct PWM runs at half the frequency of fast PWM.

The prescaler runs free and is shared; the first count after enabling can come 1 to N+1 clocks later. PSR10 resets it, and TSM holds it in reset for synchronized setup. T0 is sampled every system clock and its edge reaches the counter 2.5 to 3.5 clocks later; each half period must exceed one system clock, so the external frequency must be under fclk_I/O/2, and under fclk_I/O/2.5 is advised. An external clock cannot be prescaled.

Compares AIN0 (PB0, +) with AIN1 (PB1, -); ACO is high when AIN0 is higher, synchronized with 1-2 clocks of delay. ACBG replaces AIN0 with the bandgap. With ACME set and the ADC off, ADC0-ADC3 can replace AIN1. The interrupt fires on toggle, falling or rising output. Disable ACIE before changing ACD or ACIS bits. ACD turns the comparator off.

10-bit successive approximation ADC with four single-ended inputs (ADC0 PB5, ADC1 PB2, ADC2 PB4, ADC3 PB3), reference VCC or internal 1.1 V, input range 0 to VREF. Full resolution needs an ADC clock of 50-200 kHz from the 7-bit prescaler; higher clocks trade resolution for rate. A conversion takes 13 ADC clocks, the first after enabling 25. Single, free-running or auto-triggered conversion. Result right-adjusted, or left-adjusted with ADLAR for 8-bit reads of ADCH only; otherwise read ADCL first, then ADCH. The first result after switching reference may be wrong and should be dropped.

The sample-and-hold is about 14 pF (worst case, including stray) behind 1-100 kΩ. Sources of about 10 kΩ or less give negligible sampling error; higher impedances need more time. Filter components above fADC/2 before the input. For accuracy: short analog traces over an analog ground plane, away from fast digital lines; no switching outputs during a conversion; bypass caps close to VCC and GND; and ADC Noise Reduction mode, especially above 1 MHz system clock. Disable the digital input on ADC pins with DIDR0.

With the ADC enabled, single conversion mode and the conversion interrupt on, entering ADC Noise Reduction or Idle sleep starts a conversion once the CPU halts; the ADC interrupt then wakes the part. The ADC is not switched off automatically in other sleep modes; clear ADEN first.

Programming DWEN (with lock bits unprogrammed) turns the RESET pin into an open-drain, pulled-up, bidirectional one-wire debug link, so external reset is not available. Software breakpoints rewrite flash and shorten its retention; debugged parts should not be shipped. Changing the system clock (CLKPS) or running below 100 kHz can break communication. DWEN keeps parts of the clock system running in sleep, raising sleep current; leave it unprogrammed when not debugging. debugWIRE can read flash even with lock bits set.

SPM is enabled by the SELFPRGEN fuse. Flash is written in 16-word pages: fill the temporary buffer a word at a time (Z selects the word, R1:R0 the data), erase that page, then write it, each SPM issued within four clocks of setting SPMCSR. The CPU halts during erase and write, 3.7 ms to 4.5 ms each. The buffer clears after a page write, on CTPB or at reset, and each buffer word can be written once. An EEPROM write during loading loses the buffer. Firmware reads fuses and lock bits with RFLB + SELFPRGEN followed by LPM within three clocks: Z = 0x0000 fuse low, 0x0003 fuse high, 0x0001 lock bits.

Two lock bits, cleared only by chip erase, protect flash and EEPROM from further programming or verification and lock the fuses. Program fuses before lock bits; LB1 programmed locks the fuses. Chip erase does not change fuses. Fuse values latch on entering programming mode and at power-up; EESAVE acts as soon as it is programmed.

Flash and EEPROM are programmed over SPI (SCK PB2, MOSI PB0, MISO PB1) while RESET is held low; a valid clock per CKSEL must run. Power up with RESET and SCK low (or pulse RESET high after SCK goes low, for at least tRST plus two clocks), wait at least 20 ms, then send Programming Enable; when in sync the second byte 0x53 echoes back during the third. Data goes in on the rising SCK edge and comes out on the falling one. SCK low and high times must each exceed 2 CPU clocks below 12 MHz and 3 at or above. Flash is loaded a page at a time; EEPROM by byte (with automatic erase) or by 4-byte page. Chip erase sets all flash and EEPROM to 0xFF.

Entry: with SDI, SII and SDO low, RESET low and VCC at 0 V, apply 4.5-5.5 V to VCC so that it passes 1.8 V within 20 µs; after 20-60 µs put 11.5-12.5 V on RESET; keep the Prog_enable pins for at least 10 µs, release SDO, and wait at least 300 µs before the first instruction. If VCC rises too slowly, apply the high voltage when VCC reaches 0.9-1.1 V instead and wait for VCC to reach 4.5-5.5 V before instructions. Data is clocked on the rising SCI edge; SCI period at least 220 ns. Exit by removing power or pulling RESET to 0 V. Power-off: SCI low, RESET high, then VCC off.
Projected retention failures stay far below 1 PPM: 20 years at 85 °C, 100 years at 25 °C.
EEPROM writes can fail with VCC below 1.9 V; do not write the EEPROM below 1.9 V. Revisions E and F were not sampled; revisions A to D were sold as ATtiny13/ATtiny13V.
